Carpal tunnel syndrome

Human trials are numerous but heterogeneous; a systematic review found no pooled advantage for pain or grip strength, while functionality may improve.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

Human trials are numerous but heterogeneous; a systematic review found no pooled advantage for pain or grip strength, while functionality may improve.

Summary of the Evidence

The exact category contains 49 unique titles: 26 randomized human reports, eight nonrandomized controlled reports, three single-arm studies, and nine reviews or syntheses, alongside a protocol and laboratory record. Reviews summarize overlapping clinical trials, so publications cannot be equated with independent cohorts. Findings vary across symptoms, grip, nerve conduction, and function. (Lauxen et al. 2025)

Human and clinical evidence

Human randomized and controlled studies dominate the direct evidence. Lauxen et al. reviewed 13 randomized trials and found no pooled advantage for pain or grip strength, while functional outcomes favored PBM in some analyses. Karaman et al. found no clear additional effect when low-level laser therapy or phonophoresis was added to exercise. These results do not support a consistent effect across outcome domains. (Karaman et al. 2024)

Animal evidence

No animal clinical or laboratory species study was identified in the exact category. One record is tagged as in-vitro; it does not provide clinical evidence in patients.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

One in-vitro study is indexed.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The database records different laser and LED sources, wavelengths, powers, energy densities, and schedules. Both low-intensity PBM and higher-intensity laser approaches appear in the wider literature, and treatment is often combined with exercise, splinting, or other therapy. This variation limits protocol-level conclusions.

Interpretation

There is a broad clinical literature, but study quality, comparator choice, and outcome selection vary. Future trials should use sham control, report diagnostic criteria and nerve conduction outcomes, and distinguish standalone PBM from PBM added to exercise or splinting. Longer follow-up is needed to establish whether any short-term functional changes persist.

Evidence strength in source summaryLow for short-term hand function Very low for pain or grip-strength benefit
Publications and records49 unique titles in Carpal tunnel syndrome.

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

The database contains 49 titles, including 26 randomized human reports and nine reviews or meta-analyses. Modalities and comparators differ, and reviews overlap primary trials. Further adequately powered sham-controlled studies should report symptoms, nerve conduction, strength, function, and follow-up after treatment.
